arXiv:2010.08536v2 [nlin.SI] 03 Dec 2020

Abelian Lie symmetry algebras of two-dimensional quasilinear evolution equations

Rohollah Bakhshandeh-Chamazkoti†

† Department of Mathematics, Faculty of Basic Sciences, Babol Noshirvani University of Technology, Babol, Iran.

E-mail: r_bakhshandeh@nit.ac.ir​

We carry out the classification of abelian Lie symmetry algebras of two-dimensional second-order nondegenerate quasilinear evolution equations. It is shown that such an equation is linearizable if it admits an abelian Lie symmetry algebra that is of dimension greater than or equal to five or of dimension greater than or equal to three with rank one.

1 Introduction

Transformation properties of evolution equations especially Lie group of point symmetries has been widely studied because of many practical benefits that such knowledge gives and also because of the variety of physical applications that are modeled by these equations.

The purpose of this paper is to classify all admissible abelian symmetry algebras of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} of two-dimensional second-order non-degenerate quasilinear evolution equations, which are of the general form

ut=F⁡(t,x,y,u,ux,uy)​ux​x+G⁡(t,x,y,u,ux,uy)​uy​y+H⁡(t,x,y,u,ux,uy)​ux​y+K⁡(t,x,y,u,ux,uy),\displaystyle\begin{split}u_{t}={}&F(t,x,y,u,u_{x},u_{y})u_{xx}+G(t,x,y,u,u_{x},u_{y})u_{yy}+H(t,x,y,u,u_{x},u_{y})u_{xy}\\ {}&+K(t,x,y,u,u_{x},u_{y}),\end{split} (1)

where F,G,HF,~G,~H and KK are some non-zero smooth functions in terms of t,x,y,u,ux,uyt,x,y,u,u_{x},u_{y} variables with F​G−H2/4≠0FG-H^{2}/4\neq 0. The present paper is the first part of a project to classify Lie symmetry algebras of differential equations of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} and develops the methods which were applied in [3].

In [3], the authors gave a complete Lie point symmetry classification of all third-order evolution equations

ut=F⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x)​ux​x​x+G⁡(t,x,u,ux,ux​x),\displaystyle u_{t}=F(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx})u_{xxx}+G(t,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx}), (2)

where F≠0F\neq 0 and GG are two functions in terms of t,x,u,ux,ux​xt,x,u,u_{x},u_{xx} which (2) admit semi-simple symmetry algebras. Before in [9], this method was applied for equation (2) for F=1F=1. This method for finding symmetries and integrability properties for (1+1)(1+1)-dimension evolution equations were carried out in [1, 7, 8, 9, 13, 18, 19], and recently this method is developed in [2, 4, 10, 11, 17].

In [11], the authors carried out enhanced symmetry analysis of the two-dimensional Burgers system

{ut+u​ux+v​uy−ux​x−uy​y=0,vt+u​vx+v​vy−vx​x−vy​y=0,\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}u_{t}+uu_{x}+vu_{y}-u_{xx}-u_{yy}=0,\\ v_{t}+uv_{x}+vv_{y}-v_{xx}-v_{yy}=0,\end{array}\right.

Under the constraint v=0v=0, the second equation of the system (1) is equaled to zero and its first equation reduces to a (1+2)(1+2)-dimensional generalization of the Burgers equation

ut+u​ux−ux​x−uy​y=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+uu_{x}-u_{xx}-u_{yy}=0, (5)

which was deduced in [15] as an equation for the wave phase of two-dimensional sound simple waves in weakly dissipative flows. Therein, symmetry analysis of this equation was carried out, which included the first exhaustive study of its Lie reductions in an optimized way and the construction of several new families of its exact solutions. The group classification of (1+2)(1+2)-dimensional diffusion-convection equation (5) was also investigated in [6]. Recently, Bihlo and Popovych in [5], classified zeroth-order conservation laws of systems from the class of two-dimensional shallow water equations with variable bottom topography.

The present paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is presented to some basic definitions of equivalence groupoid and then we show the infinitesimal Lie point symmetry of differential equations of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}}, has the form

Q=a(t)∂t+b(t,x,y,u)∂x+c(t,x,y,u)∂y+φ(t,x,y,u)∂u,Q=a(t)\partial_{t}+b(t,x,y,u)\partial_{x}+c(t,x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y,u)\partial_{u},

where a⁡(t),b⁡(t,x,y,u),c⁡(t,x,y,u)a(t),\;b(t,x,y,u),\;c(t,x,y,u) and φ⁡(t,x,y,u)\varphi(t,x,y,u) are smooth functions of their arguments which QQ is equal to ∂t\partial_{t} or ∂u\partial_{u} as a canonical form under the equivalence group (8) and also the ∂x,∂y\partial_{x},\partial_{y} and ∂u\partial_{u} are equivalent as canonical forms under this equivalence group (8).

In section 3, we compute the determining equations by applying Lie symmetry conditions.

In section 4, we classify the admissible abelian symmetry algebras and we prove that any equation of the the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} equipped with an five-dimensional abelian symmetry algebra or with dimension bigger than five, or three-dimensional abelain Lie algebra or with dimension bigger than three with rank-one realization, is linearizable. Finally, a table included some invariant solutions corresponding to abelian Lie symmetries for non-linear cases of the evolution equation is listed.

2 Equivalence groupoid

Let ℒθ{\mathcal{L}}_{\theta} denote a system of differential equations of the form L⁡(x,u(r),θ(q)​(x,u(r)))=0L(x,u^{(r)},\theta^{(q)}(x,u^{(r)}))=0, where x,ux,u, and u(r)u^{(r)} are the tuples of independent variables, of dependent variables and of derivatives of uu with respect to xx up to order rr. The tuple of functions L=(L1,…,Ll)L=(L^{1},\dots,L^{l}) of (x,u(r),θ)(x,u^{(r)},\theta) is fixed whereas the tuple of functions θ=(θ1,…,θk)\theta=(\theta^{1},\dots,\theta^{k}) of (x,u(r))(x,u^{(r)}) runs through the solution set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of an auxiliary system of differential equations and inequalities in θ\theta, where xx and u(r)u^{(r)} jointly play the role of independent variables. Thus, the class of (systems of) differential equations ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is the parameterized family of systems ℒθ{\mathcal{L}}_{\theta} with θ\theta running through the set 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The components of θ\theta are called the arbitrary elements of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}}. The equivalence groupoid 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim} of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} consists of admissible transformations of this class,

𝒢∼=𝒢∼(ℒ)={(θ,ξ,θ~)∣θ,θ~∈𝒮,ξ∈T(θ,θ~)}.\mathcal{G}^{\sim}=\mathcal{G}^{\sim}(\mathcal{L})=\big\{(\theta,\xi,\tilde{\theta})\mid\theta,\tilde{\theta}\in\mathcal{S},\xi\in\mathrm{T}(\theta,\tilde{\theta})\big\}.

Here ℒθ{\mathcal{L}}_{\theta} and ℒθ~{\mathcal{L}}_{\tilde{\theta}} are the source and the target systems, belonging to the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} and corresponding to the values θ\theta and θ~\tilde{\theta} of the arbitrary-element tuple, respectively, which in turn runs through the solution set 𝒮\mathcal{S} of the auxiliary system SS of equations and inequalities for arbitrary elements, and ξ\xi is a point transformation relating the equations ℒθ{\mathcal{L}}_{\theta} and ℒθ~{\mathcal{L}}_{\tilde{\theta}} (the set of all such transformations is denoted by T⁡(θ,θ~)\mathrm{T}(\theta,\tilde{\theta})) [16].

Definition 1.

The (usual) equivalence group G∼=G∼​(ℒ)G^{\sim}=G^{\sim}(\mathcal{L}) of the class ℒ\mathcal{L} is the (pseudo)group of point transformations in the space of (x,u(r),θ)(x,u^{(r)},\theta) which are projectable to the space of (x,u(r′))(x,u^{(r^{\prime})}) for any 0≤r′≤r0\leq r^{\prime}\leq r, are consistent with the contact structure on the space of (x,u(r))(x,u^{(r)}) and preserve the class ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Definition 2.

The class of differential equations ℒ{\mathcal{L}} is called normalized if its equivalence groupoid 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim} is induced by its equivalence group G∼G^{\sim}, meaning that for any triple (θ,ξ,θ~)(\theta,\xi,\tilde{\theta}) from 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}, there exists a transformation Ξ\Xi from G∼G^{\sim} such that θ~=Ξ∗​θ\tilde{\theta}=\Xi_{*}\theta and ξ=Ξ|(x,u)\xi=\Xi|_{(x,u)}.

For the class ℒ\mathcal{L} of equations of the form (1), the tuple θ\theta of arbitrary elements is constituted by four arbitrary smooth functions FF, GG, HH and KK of (t,x,y,u,ut,ux,uy)(t,x,y,u,u_{t},u_{x},u_{y}) that satisfy the auxiliary system SS consisting of the single inequality F​G−H2/4≠0FG-H^{2}/4\neq 0, that is, θ=(F,G,H,K)\theta=(F,G,H,K) and 𝒮={(F,G,H,K)∣F​G−H2/4≠0}\mathcal{S}=\{(F,G,H,K)\mid FG-H^{2}/4\neq 0\}. The usual equivalence group 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim} of the class ℒ\mathcal{L} can be assumed to act in the space with coordinates (t,x,y,u,ut,ux,uy,F,G,H,K)(t,x,y,u,u_{t},u_{x},u_{y},F,G,H,K) and to consist of the point transformations of the form

In other words, Theorem 3 means that the equivalence groupoid 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim} of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} consists of of the triples (θ,ξ,θ~)(\theta,\xi,\tilde{\theta}), where the point transformations ξ\xi is of the form (8), the tuples θ\theta runs through the entire set 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and the tuples θ~\tilde{\theta} are defined by the equations (9)–(12). Thus, the equivalence groupoid 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim} can be partitioned into families of admissible transformations each of which corresponds to a fixed point transformations ξ\xi and parameterized by arbitrary values of θ∈𝒮\theta\in\mathcal{S}. This means that the each point transformation of the form (8) is the projection of an equivalence transformation to the space with coordinates (t,x,y,u)(t,x,y,u), the (F,G,H,K)(F,G,H,K)-components of this equivalence transformation are defined by the equations (9), (10), (11) and (12), respectively, and the action groupoid of the equivalence group G∼G^{\sim} of the class ℒ{\mathcal{L}} coincides with the entire equivalence groupoid 𝒢∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim} of this class. As a result, we have the following theorem.

Theorem 4.

The classℒ{\mathcal{L}} of equations of the form (1) with F​G−H2/4≠0FG-H^{2}/4\neq 0 is normalized in the usual sense. Its usual equivalence group G∼G^{\sim} is constituted by the point transformations in the space with coordinates (t,x,y,u,ut,ux,uy,F,G,H,K)(t,x,y,u,u_{t},u_{x},u_{y},F,G,H,K), where the (t,x,y,u)(t,x,y,u)-components are given by (8), the (ut,ux,uy)(u_{t},u_{x},u_{y})-components are computed using the chain rule, and the (F,G,H,K)(F,G,H,K)-components are defined by the equations (9), (10), (11) and (12), respectively.

Corollary 5.

A smooth vector field QQ which defines an infinitesimal point symmetry of equation (1), has the form

Q=a(t)∂t+b(t,x,y,u)∂x+c(t,x,y,u)∂y+φ(t,x,y,u)∂u.\displaystyle Q=a(t)\partial_{t}+b(t,x,y,u)\partial_{x}+c(t,x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y,u)\partial_{u}. (25)

where a⁡(t),b⁡(t,x,y,u),c⁡(t,x,y,u),φ⁡(t,x,y,u)a(t),\;b(t,x,y,u),\;c(t,x,y,u),\;\varphi(t,x,y,u) are smooth functions of their arguments.

Theorem 6.

A vector field

Q=a(t)∂t+b(t,x,y,u)∂x+c(t,x,y,u)∂y+φ(t,x,y,u)∂uQ=a(t)\partial_{t}+b(t,x,y,u)\partial_{x}+c(t,x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y,u)\partial_{u}

can be transformed by transformations of the form (8) into one of the following canonical forms:

Q=∂t,Q=∂u.Q=\partial_{t},\qquad Q=\partial_{u}. (26)
Proof.

Any operator

Q=a(t)∂t+b(t,x,y,u)∂x+c(t,x,y,u)∂y+φ(t,x,y,u)∂u,Q=a(t)\partial_{t}+b(t,x,y,u)\partial_{x}+c(t,x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y,u)\partial_{u},

is transformed by our allowed transformations into Q′=Q(T)∂t′+Q(X)∂x′+Q(Y)∂y′+Q(U)∂u′Q^{\prime}=Q(T)\partial_{t^{\prime}}+Q(X)\partial_{x^{\prime}}+Q(Y)\partial_{y^{\prime}}+Q(U)\partial_{u^{\prime}}. If a⁡(t)≠0a(t)\neq 0 then we choose T⁡(t)T(t) so that Q⁡(T)=a⁡(t)​T˙​(t)=1Q(T)=a(t)\dot{T}(t)=1 (at least locally) and also we can choose X,YX,~Y and UU to be each of any three independent integrals of the PDE Q⁡(V)=0Q(V)=0. This gives the canonical form Q=∂tQ=\partial_{t} in some coordinate system. If we now have a⁡(t)=0a(t)=0 then QQ is transformed into Q′=Q(X)∂x′+Q(Y)∂y′+Q(U)∂u′Q^{\prime}=Q(X)\partial_{x^{\prime}}+Q(Y)\partial_{y^{\prime}}+Q(U)\partial_{u^{\prime}}. We then choose X,YX,~Y and UU so that Q⁡(X)=Q⁡(Y)=0,Q⁡(U)=1Q(X)=Q(Y)=0,\;\;Q(U)=1. This gives us the canonical form Q=∂uQ=\partial_{u} in some coordinate system. ∎

Remark 7.

It is sometimes useful to use the fact that t′=t,x′=y′=u,u′=x=yt^{\prime}=t,\;\,x^{\prime}=y^{\prime}=u,\;\;u^{\prime}=x=y is an equivalence transformation preserving the form of equation (1), and it gives us the following transformations of derivatives:

∂t↔∂t,∂x↔∂y,∂x↔∂u,∂y↔∂u.\partial_{t}\leftrightarrow\partial_{t},\quad\partial_{x}\leftrightarrow\partial_{y},\quad\partial_{x}\leftrightarrow\partial_{u},\quad\partial_{y}\leftrightarrow\partial_{u}.

4 Abelian Lie algebras as symmetries

Theorem 9.

There are only two inequivalent forms for one-dimensional abelian Lie symmetry algebras A=⟨∂t⟩A=\langle\partial_{t}\rangle and A=⟨∂u⟩A=\langle\partial_{u}\rangle.

Theorem 10.

All inequivalent, admissible two-dimensional abelian Lie symmetry algebras are ⟨∂t,∂u⟩\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂x,∂u⟩\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{u}\rangle and ⟨∂u,x∂u⟩\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u}\rangle.

Proof.

Now we take dimA=2\dim A=2. We have A=⟨Q1,Q2⟩A=\langle Q_{1},Q_{2}\rangle. For rank​A=1\text{rank}\,A=1 the case Q1=∂tQ_{1}=\partial_{t} is impossible because it leads to Q2=a(t)∂tQ_{2}=a(t)\partial_{t} and [Q1,Q2]=0[Q_{1},Q_{2}]=0 gives a˙​(t)=0\dot{a}(t)=0, so dimA=1\dim A=1. We take Q1=∂uQ_{1}=\partial_{u} and Q2=φ(t,x,y)∂uQ_{2}=\varphi(t,x,y)\partial_{u}. The residual equivalence group G∼(∂u)G^{\sim}(\partial_{u}) is given by

t′=T⁡(t),x′=X⁡(t,x,y),y′=Y⁡(t,x,y),u′=u+U⁡(t,x,y)t^{\prime}=T(t),\,x^{\prime}=X(t,x,y),\,y^{\prime}=Y(t,x,y),\,u^{\prime}=u+U(t,x,y)

where T˙​(t)​(Xx​Yy−Xy​Yx)≠0\dot{T}(t)\left(X_{x}Y_{y}-X_{y}Y_{x}\right)\neq 0. Under such a transformation Q2Q_{2} is mapped to Q2′=φ(t,x,y)∂u′Q^{\prime}_{2}=\varphi(t,x,y)\partial_{u^{\prime}}. If φx≠0\varphi_{x}\neq 0 (or φy≠0\varphi_{y}\neq 0) we may take X⁡(t,x,y)=φ⁡(t,x,y)X(t,x,y)=\varphi(t,x,y) so that the Q′2=x′∂u′Q^{\prime}_{2}=x^{\prime}\partial_{u^{\prime}} and then we have ⟨∂u,x∂u⟩\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u}\rangle in canonical form. If φx=φy=0\varphi_{x}=\varphi_{y}=0 then Q2=φ(t)∂uQ_{2}=\varphi(t)\partial_{u}. Substituting ∂u\partial_{u} and φ(t)∂u\varphi(t)\partial_{u} into the equation (33b) we find Gu=0,φ˙​(t)=0G_{u}=0,\;\dot{\varphi}(t)=0 so φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) is a constant and thus dimA=1\dim A=1 which is a contradiction, so we have no admissible canonical form in this case.

If dimA=2,rank​A=2\dim A=2,\;\text{rank}\,A=2 then we may take Q1=∂tQ_{1}=\partial_{t} or Q1=∂uQ_{1}=\partial_{u}. If Q1=∂tQ_{1}=\partial_{t} then, by commutativity and the fact that A=⟨Q1,Q2⟩A=\langle Q_{1},Q_{2}\rangle, we may take Q2=b(x,y,u)∂x+c(x,y,u)∂y+φ(x,y,u)∂uQ_{2}=b(x,y,u)\partial_{x}+c(x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi(x,y,u)\partial_{u}. The residual equivalence group G∼(∂t)G^{\sim}(\partial_{t}) consists of invertible transformations of the form

t′=t+l,x′=X(x,,y,u),y′=Y(x,,y,u),u′=U(x,y,u)t^{\prime}=t+l,\;x^{\prime}=X(x,,y,u),\;y^{\prime}=Y(x,,y,u),\;u^{\prime}=U(x,y,u)

where l=constantl=\text{constant}. Under such a transformation Q2Q_{2} is mapped to Q2′=Q2(X)∂x′+Q2(Y)∂y′+Q2(U)∂u′Q^{\prime}_{2}=Q_{2}(X)\partial_{x^{\prime}}+Q_{2}(Y)\partial_{y^{\prime}}+Q_{2}(U)\partial_{u^{\prime}}. We can always choose X,YX,\,Y and UU so that Q2​(U)=1,Q2​(X)=Q2​(Y)=0Q_{2}(U)=1,\;Q_{2}(X)=Q_{2}(Y)=0. Thus we have the canonical form ⟨∂t,∂u⟩\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u}\rangle. If we take Q1=∂uQ_{1}=\partial_{u}, then we have Q2=a(t)∂t+b(t,x,y)∂x+c(t,x,y)∂y+φ(t,x,y)∂uQ_{2}=a(t)\partial_{t}+b(t,x,y)\partial_{x}+c(t,x,y)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y)\partial_{u}. The residual equivalence group G∼(∂u)G^{\sim}(\partial_{u}) is the group of transformations

t′=T⁡(t),x′=X⁡(t,x,y),y′=Y⁡(t,x,y),u′=u+U⁡(t,x,y)t^{\prime}=T(t),\,x^{\prime}=X(t,x,y),\,y^{\prime}=Y(t,x,y),\,u^{\prime}=u+U(t,x,y)

with T˙​(t)​(Xx​Yy−Xy​Yx)≠0\dot{T}(t)\left(X_{x}Y_{y}-X_{y}Y_{x}\right)\neq 0. Under such a transformation, Q2Q_{2} is mapped to

If a⁡(t)≠0a(t)\neq 0, we may choose T⁡(t),X⁡(t,x,y),Y⁡(t,x,y)T(t),\,X(t,x,y),\,Y(t,x,y) and U⁡(t,x,y)U(t,x,y) so that a⁡(t)​T˙​(t)=1,Q2​(X)=0,Q2​(Y)=0,a(t)\dot{T}(t)=1,\,Q_{2}(X)=0,\,Q_{2}(Y)=0, and φ+Q2​(U)=0\varphi+Q_{2}(U)=0. Then we may take Q1=∂u,Q2=∂tQ_{1}=\partial_{u},\,Q_{2}=\partial_{t}. If, however, a⁡(t)=0a(t)=0, then Q2=b(t,x,y)∂x+c(t,x,y)∂y+φ(t,x,y)∂uQ_{2}=b(t,x,y)\partial_{x}+c(t,x,y)\partial_{y}+\varphi(t,x,y)\partial_{u} and we then have b2+c2≠0b^{2}+c^{2}\neq 0 since we have rank​A=2{\rm rank}\,A=2. Then

Q2′=[b(t,x,y)Xx+c(t,x,y)Xy]∂x′+[b(t,x,y)Yx+c(t,x,y)Yy]∂y′+[φ+b(t,x,y)Ux+c(t,x,y)Uy]∂u′Q^{\prime}_{2}=[b(t,x,y)X_{x}+c(t,x,y)X_{y}]\partial_{x^{\prime}}+[b(t,x,y)Y_{x}+c(t,x,y)Y_{y}]\partial_{y^{\prime}}+[\varphi+b(t,x,y)U_{x}+c(t,x,y)U_{y}]\partial_{u^{\prime}}

and because b2+c2≠0b^{2}+c^{2}\neq 0 we may choose X⁡(t,x,y),Y⁡(t,x,y)X(t,x,y),\;Y(t,x,y) and U⁡(t,x,y)U(t,x,y) so that

φ+b⁡(t,x,y)​Ux+c⁡(t,x,y)​Uy=0,b⁡(t,x,y)​Yx+c⁡(t,x,y)​Yy=0,b⁡(t,x,y)​Xx+c⁡(t,x,y)​Xy=1\varphi+b(t,x,y)U_{x}+c(t,x,y)U_{y}=0,\;b(t,x,y)Y_{x}+c(t,x,y)Y_{y}=0,\;b(t,x,y)X_{x}+c(t,x,y)X_{y}=1

and Q4=b4(x,y,u)∂x+c4(x,y,u)∂y+φ4(x,y,u)∂uQ_{4}=b_{4}(x,y,u)\partial_{x}+c_{4}(x,y,u)\partial_{y}+\varphi_{4}(x,y,u)\partial_{u}. with Yy≠0Y_{y}\neq 0. Since dimA=4\dim A=4 then we have by2+φy2≠0b_{y}^{2}+\varphi_{y}^{2}\neq 0. So there are no admissible abelian Lie algebras AA with dimA≥4,rank​A=3\dim A\geq 4,\,{\rm rank}\,A=3.

For dimA=4,rank​A=2\dim A=4,\,{\rm rank}\,A=2 we may take Q1=∂t,Q2=∂u,Q3=x∂uQ_{1}=\partial_{t},\,Q_{2}=\partial_{u},\,Q_{3}=x\partial_{u}, and for Q4Q_{4} we take Q4=φ(x,y)∂uQ_{4}=\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u} because AA is abelian and rank​A=2{\rm rank}\,A=2. Further φy≠0\varphi_{y}\neq 0, for otherwise Q4Q_{4} would be a constant linear combination of Q2Q_{2} and Q3Q_{3}, contradicting dimA=4\dim A=4. Thus we have A=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,φ(x,y)∂u⟩A=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle with φy≠0\varphi_{y}\neq 0. The residual equivalence group G∼(∂t,∂u,x∂u)G^{\sim}(\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u}) is given by transformations of the form

t′=t+k,x′=x,y′=Y⁡(x,y),u′=u+U⁡(x,y)t^{\prime}=t+k,\;x^{\prime}=x,\;y^{\prime}=Y(x,y),\;u^{\prime}=u+U(x,y)

with Yy≠0Y_{y}\neq 0. Under this transformation Q4Q_{4} maps to Q4′=φ(x,y)∂u′Q^{\prime}_{4}=\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u}^{\prime} and since φy≠0\varphi_{y}\neq 0 we may choose φ⁡(x,y)=Y⁡(x,y)\varphi(x,y)=Y(x,y). Thus Q4=y∂uQ_{4}=y\partial_{u} and A=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,y∂u⟩A=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u}\rangle.

For dimA=5,rank​A=2\dim A=5,\;\text{rank}\,A=2 we find that any additional symmetry operator QQ must be of the form Q=φ(x,y)∂uQ=\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u} with φy≠0\varphi_{y}\neq 0 and, substituting the vector fields a symmetries in the (33) equations gives φx​y​K+φy​y​G+φx​x​F=0\varphi_{xy}K+\varphi_{yy}G+\varphi_{xx}F=0 with φx​y2+φy​y2+φx​x2≠0\varphi_{xy}^{2}+\varphi_{yy}^{2}+\varphi_{xx}^{2}\neq 0. From this it follows that φx≠0,φy≠0\varphi_{x}\neq 0,\varphi_{y}\neq 0 and then φx​y≠0\varphi_{xy}\neq 0. Hence we find A=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,y∂u,φ(x,y)∂u⟩A=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u},\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle with φx​y≠0\varphi_{xy}\neq 0. For dimA≥5,rank​A=2\dim A\geq 5,\;\text{rank}\,A=2, arguments similar to those for dimA=5,rank​A=2\dim A=5,\,\text{rank}\,A=2 give us abelian Lie algebras

A=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,y∂u,φ(x,y)∂u,q1(x,y)∂u,…,qk(x,y)∂u⟩\displaystyle A=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u},\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u},q_{1}(x,y)\partial_{u},\ldots,q_{k}(x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle (35)

with the sole proviso that each of the q:q: s satisfy qx​y≠0q_{xy}\neq 0 and

φx​x​F+φy​y​Gφx​y=qx​x​F+qy​y​Gqx​y,\frac{\varphi_{xx}F+\varphi_{yy}G}{\varphi_{xy}}=\frac{q_{xx}F+q_{yy}G}{q_{xy}},

as well as linear independence of the vector fields (35). We obtain equations of the form

ut=F⁡(x,y)​ux​x+G⁡(x,y)​uy​y+H⁡(x,y)​ux​y−φy​y​G+φx​x​Fφx​y,\displaystyle u_{t}=F(x,y)u_{xx}+G(x,y)u_{yy}+H(x,y)u_{xy}-\frac{\varphi_{yy}G+\varphi_{xx}F}{\varphi_{xy}}, (36)

with φx​y≠0,φx​x2+φy​y2≠0\varphi_{xy}\neq 0,\;\varphi_{xx}^{2}+\varphi_{yy}^{2}\neq 0.

For dimA≥4,rank​A=1\dim A\geq 4,\;\text{rank}\,A=1, arguments similar to those for dimA=3,rank​A=1\dim A=3,\,\text{rank}\,A=1 give us abelian Lie algebras AA of the form

A=⟨∂u,x∂u,y∂u,φ(t,x,y)∂u,q1(t,x,y)∂u,…,qk(t,x,y)∂u⟩\displaystyle A=\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u},\varphi(t,x,y)\partial_{u},q_{1}(t,x,y)\partial_{u},\dots,q_{k}(t,x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle (37)

with the sole proviso that each of the q:q: s satisfy qx​x​(t,x,y)≠0,φ⁡(t,x,y)≠0q_{xx}(t,x,y)\neq 0,\varphi(t,x,y)\neq 0 and

φt−φy​y​G−φx​y​Kφx​x=qt−qy​y​G−qx​y​Kqx​x,\frac{\varphi_{t}-\varphi_{yy}G-\varphi_{xy}K}{\varphi_{xx}}=\frac{q_{t}-q_{yy}G-q_{xy}K}{q_{xx}},

as well as linear independence of the vector fields (37). We obtain equations of the form

ut=[φt−φy​y​G−φx​y​Kφx​x]​ux​x+G⁡(t,x,y)​uy​y+H⁡(t,x,y)​ux​y+K⁡(t,x,y).\displaystyle u_{t}=\left[\frac{\varphi_{t}-\varphi_{yy}G-\varphi_{xy}K}{\varphi_{xx}}\right]u_{xx}+G(t,x,y)u_{yy}+H(t,x,y)u_{xy}+K(t,x,y). (38)

∎

We have the following corollary of the above results:

Corollary 13.

The evolution equations of the form (1) admitting abelian Lie algebras 𝖠\mathsf{A} with dim𝖠≥5\dim\mathsf{A}\geq 5 or if dim𝖠≥3,rank​𝖠=1\dim\mathsf{A}\geq 3,\;\;{\rm rank}\,\mathsf{A}=1 as symmetries are linearizable.

Proof.

The proof is just by calculation: for dim𝖠≥3,rank​𝖠=1\dim\mathsf{A}\geq 3,\;{\rm rank}\,\mathsf{A}=1 we find the evolution equations (34) and (38) which is linear in uu and its derivatives. Similarly, the rank-two algebra

A=⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,y∂u,φ(x,y)∂u,q1(x,y)∂u,…,qk(x,y)∂u⟩,withφx​y≠0,(qi)x​y≠0,A=\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u},\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u},q_{1}(x,y)\partial_{u},\dots,q_{k}(x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle,\;\;{\rm with}\;\;\varphi_{xy}\neq 0,\,(q_{i})_{xy}\neq 0,

gives the (36) equation. ∎

5 Conclusion and future work

We have carried out the abelain Lie symmetry classification of evolution equation (1). There are just two inequivalent forms for one–dimensional abelian Lie symmetry algebras ⟨∂t⟩,⟨∂u⟩\langle\partial_{t}\rangle,\;\langle\partial_{u}\rangle and three inequivalent forms for two–dimensional ⟨∂t,∂u⟩,⟨∂x,∂u⟩,⟨∂u,x∂u⟩\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u}\rangle,\;\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{u}\rangle,\;\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u}\rangle. For three–dimensional we have ⟨∂t,∂x,∂u⟩,\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{x},\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u⟩,\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂u,x∂u,y∂u⟩,\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂x,∂y,∂u⟩,\langle\partial_{x},\partial_{y},\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂u,x∂u,φ(t,x)∂u⟩\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},\varphi(t,x)\partial_{u}\rangle with φx​x≠0\varphi_{xx}\neq 0 abelian Lie symmetry algebras. We have four inequivalent four–dimensional admissible abelian Lie symmetry algebras ⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,y∂u⟩,\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂t,∂x,∂u,y∂u⟩,\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{x},\partial_{u},y\partial_{u}\rangle, ⟨∂t,∂x,∂u,y∂x⟩,\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{x},\partial_{u},y\partial_{x}\rangle, ⟨∂t,∂x,∂y,∂u⟩\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{x},\partial_{y},\partial_{u}\rangle and for admissible abelian Lie symmetry algebras with dimension bigger than four are

⟨∂u,x∂u,y∂u,φ(t,x,y)∂u,q1(t,x,y)∂u,…,qk(t,x,y)∂u⟩,withφx​x≠0,(qi)x​x≠0,\displaystyle\langle\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u},\varphi(t,x,y)\partial_{u},q_{1}(t,x,y)\partial_{u},\dots,q_{k}(t,x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle,\;{\rm with}\;\;\varphi_{xx}\neq 0,\,(q_{i})_{xx}\neq 0,
⟨∂t,∂u,x∂u,y∂u,φ(x,y)∂u,q1(x,y)∂u,…,qk(x,y)∂u⟩,withφx​y≠0,(qi)x​y≠0.\displaystyle\langle\partial_{t},\partial_{u},x\partial_{u},y\partial_{u},\varphi(x,y)\partial_{u},q_{1}(x,y)\partial_{u},\dots,q_{k}(x,y)\partial_{u}\rangle,\;\;{\rm with}\;\;\varphi_{xy}\neq 0,\,(q_{i})_{xy}\neq 0.

The evolution equations of the form (1) admitting five-dimensional abelian Lie algebras or with a dimension higher than five or if with three-dimensional abelian Lie algebras or with a dimension higher than three with rank-one as symmetries are linearizable.

In future work, we show the evolution equations (1) admit 𝔰​𝔩​(2,ℝ){\mathfrak{s}}{\mathfrak{l}}(2,{\mathbb{R}}) as semi-simple symmetry algebras we classify these realizations.
